report: Conclusion: the claim is overstated. Human evidence does not show a reliable, clinically meaningful reduction in abdominal fat from CLA. A 2007 meta-analysis found CLA produced only small average fat-mass losses (about 0.05 kg/week at ~3.2 g/day), with heterogeneity and uncertain relevance (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17490954/?ref=myhealthgoat.com). A later systematic review of long-term randomized trials concluded evidence was insufficient to support CLA for body-weight/fat reduction (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00394-011-0253-9). One small RCT in abdominally obese men reported reduced abdominal adipose tissue, but it was short, selective, and not a basis for general claims (https://www.nature.com/articles/0801659?error=cookies_not_supported&code=bc690e95-ab85-4b08-860b-6503f8979d65). NIH’s weight-loss supplement fact sheet summarizes CLA as having modest/inconsistent effects and notes safety limits, including GI effects and possible adverse metabolic signals with some isomers (https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/WeightLoss-HealthProfessional/). Overall: CLA may shift total fat mass slightly in some trials, but “reduces abdominal fat” is not well supported as a dependable benefit; diet, activity, sleep, and clinically supervised weight management have stronger evidence.
